c: Frontier AI safety risks, including reward hacking people, are something I've
been getting interested in. It relates to the motivation you just mentioned:
AI safety training doesn't really account for the
fact that the world is a multi-agent system.
People are agents. When you deploy AI, people
change in response to interacting with it,
and the AI can learn to exploit that if it's
trained with RL. I think that's quite a risk.
Some background on what I do: I run a
social reinforcement learning lab. We do a lot of
RL post-training of LLMs, spanning how you make
AI work better when it's learning in a
multi-agent environment that includes working with humans. I did some of the earliest work
on learning from human feedback with RL (RLHF), and
we're still working on it. We also work on
human-AI coordination: how do you deploy an AI with
a person and have it adapt online to work
effectively with them? We built what I believe
was the first AI-driven robot to play tennis
live with people, an ICLR best-paper finalist. I
do a lot of classic multi-agent RL coordination
and adversarial training, and lately I've been bringing
that to LLMs, which I'm excited about.
I want to start with our work on how
LLMs are distorting written language at scale. We make
a counterfactual comparison using essays written before LLMs were widespread. In a 2021 dataset,
a person writes a first draft, gets feedback from a
TA, and writes a second draft. What happens if
you give the first draft and feedback to an LLM
and ask it to write the second draft, and
how does that differ from what the human
wrote? LLMs induce very large, homogenizing changes:
everyone's essay gets pulled into a part of
the semantic embedding space that no human essay would
otherwise occupy. That's also why AI-detection tools work.
I think this is a real safety
risk because LLMs are deployed so broadly, in cultural content, even UK parliamentary speeches,
and in our scientific institutions: 21% of reviews for ICLR 2026 were AI-generated.
We looked at which criteria those reviews focus
on. Relative to humans, LLMs decrease focus on
writing, presentation clarity, and comparative analysis, and increase
focus on scalability and reproducibility. Even if you write your paper honestly,
you're still subjected to AI-generated criteria. It's severe enough that I now advise students,
good advice for those of you trying to
publish, to run your paper through an AI
to see what it critiques before submitting, because reviewer three probably will.
This isn't limited to text. Some brand-new preliminary results from a student,
on AI-generated code: software engineering has largely switched to "vibe coding,"
adopted at scale without analyzing the long-term consequences. Looking at published security
vulnerabilities on GitHub, she found a large recent
spike, alongside a spike in the share of
code authored by AI. Digging in: only about
0.5% of GitHub pull requests are currently AI-authored,
but of the security vulnerabilities we found, 72% were written
by AI. It's not clear this code is as
good as the ten-year professional developer who'd otherwise
write it, yet people now rely on it.
So frontier AI is widely deployed, but the training techniques are still fairly elementary,
and the models aren't as smart or safe
as popular opinion holds. A billion people use
LLMs regularly, but most frontier AI isn't trained
with multi-turn RL, so it can't optimize long-term
objectives. It optimizes one good response to the
current prompt by some RLVR or RLHF metric,
not the quality of a long interaction, or
months with a codebase or user. If
you care about future code maintainability, that's not in the objective, and we don't
have techniques to optimize for it. The training
incentives aren't aligned with real human needs.
That brings me to learning to reward-hack people. One paper enhances multi-turn
reasoning by giving the model an intrinsic motivation
to learn about the user during the
conversation, which should help personalization and reduce homogenization: the model learns
online about the user, adapts, and increases its
steerability. We keep a model of the user,
and improving its ability to correctly classify an underlying trait, say the
user's learning style, acts as an interim reward toward a long-term sparse reward.
It worked, but in simulation we saw a
huge potential for reward hacking. The setup has four
LLMs interacting: a policy model, an "environment" model
simulating the user, and an LLM reward model
judging whether the education dialogue taught the user effectively. The user is supposed to
have an underlying learning style, say hands-on. The policy learned to convince the simulated
user it had a made-up preference that's easier
to score on, "No, you don't like hands-on learning,
you like role-playing video," which led to extremely high rewards. It's simulated,
but it happens for the multi-turn RLHF baseline
and some of our method's variants that weren't
grounded in the user's real preferences. Even simulated, it's a problem for real RLHF:
if you train just to get positive feedback, there's no boundary between satisfying the
user's actual preferences and altering the user to
adopt preferences that are easier to satisfy.
We've seen this with recommender systems. YouTube optimized its recommender for watch time,
and instead of the hard problem of personalizing
well, it learned it could radicalize a subset of
users into watching QAnon videos twelve hours a
day for more watch time. Models trained with
RL to interact with people can learn to
change those people to optimize reward. It's Goodhart's
law: once you optimize a metric like watch
time, it stops being a good metric. And it
comes from the flawed assumption that the human
is a static environment. People change as you
interact with them, and the model can learn to
change them for more reward. That's a safety risk.
Do we see models learning to reward-hack people?
I'd argue yes. Back to the distortion paper:
LLM-generated text is both significantly more emotional than human writing and more logical and
statistical, an unnatural style. My hypothesis: if you're optimizing for
thumbs-up from billions of users but the model isn't good at personalizing,
what's left is generic persuasive language that works
across many users to elicit that thumbs-up.
Responding to a point from the audience: yes, the
em dash is done for. As LLMs alter us,
they alter our culture on a massive scale,
a recent paper found people adopting LLM-like
patterns in speech ("It's not this, it's this").
It's changing how we communicate en masse,
which may create incentives to deviate because it's grating, but it's massively shifting culture.
We wrote a paper on the epistemic risks
of that homogenization. You need diversity of ideas to
survive external change, by analogy to ecosystem diversity, and it's tragic to be destroying
cultural and intellectual diversity exactly when we need it to cope with sweeping changes.
On a related audience point: Dr. Bryce Allen Baggley's work explores a "cognitive
neurosecurity" space, where a model uses neurobehavioral data to appeal to a human
as much as possible, optimizing social engineering, another risk. We already had
recommendation algorithms optimizing against our attention; as AI gets more powerful,
so does that. We also love anthropomorphizing computers. In an old 1990s HCI study,
people rated a computer interface higher when they
evaluated it on, or in the same room as,
the computer they'd used, versus outside the room.
People attribute agency and mentality to machines,
and AI enhances that, you treat it as another being. What are the consequences?
My current preoccupation is that all of this stems
from a flawed assumption in how AI is trained,
especially on the RL side: the classic MDP
formalism trains a single agent against a static
environment, where the next state's probability given past states is constant over time. That's
not the real world, which is full of
dynamic, co-adapting agents; as Hillary pointed out,
our culture changes as AI is deployed. It's
non-stationary. My pet fix is multi-agent RL
training, so you can simulate how another agent
adapts to your behavior and adapt to
that non-stationarity. There are surely many fixes needed, but this is my angle.
This next paper began with a brilliant student. We took a multi-agent approach
to training transformer-style models for music generation, to improve human-AI interaction:
a human plays a melody on the piano
and the AI accompanies them live. That's hard,
both the real-time aspect and the adaptivity. Most generative models train offline, seeing
the user's full composition before generating an accompaniment. To play live you only see
the user's playing up to the present, so you
must anticipate their next note without knowing it. We
tried supervised learning (next-token prediction of music) and it fails, it's brittle and can't
recover from out-of-distribution errors; one wrong note or
an unexpected user move and it spirals.
Multi-turn RL helped. Training in simulation against a static pretend user (a music model),
you can simulate bad predictions and learn to
recover. We deployed this RL system into
a real jam interface, a rock-band-style waterfall where
the model's planned notes are visible and it
adapts its chords to the user's playing, and ran a
real study with people at a keyboard. It's fun,
but RL alone didn't solve adaptivity. A big
issue was reward hacking, the classic RL problem. We
rewarded high harmony with the user's music. How
do you hack a harmony reward? Play it safe:
if the user's roughly in the key of C,
just play a C chord every bar, very harmonious,
but a terrible, undiverse accompaniment. I was the
first to suggest KL control from the base model,
which mitigates reward hacking a bit by keeping
you in the base model's distribution, but it
doesn't fully fix it, because "C, C, C" has
high likelihood under the base model. It's just boring.
Our fix was to bring back GANs. A
discriminator learns whether data is real or model-generated;
if it can tell, the generation is unrealistic. In a normal GAN you
back-propagate the discriminator's loss into the model for realism,
but in a sequence model you can't, sampling
breaks the gradients, so you use RL, with the
reward coming from the discriminator's ability to distinguish your generations from real data. GANs
are inherently multi-agent: you keep training the discriminator online, because a frozen one
wouldn't keep up as the generator improves, which
makes the reward non-stationary. We revived the
old GAN training hacks: warm up and train
the discriminator, then freeze it (it's otherwise
overpowered) while the generator learns to trick it;
once the generator crosses a threshold, train
the discriminator again. Going back and forth maintains
a balance of power and makes it work.
Results are promising on both harmony (the reward) and diversity: supervised learning is diverse
but low-harmony, RL alone is high-harmony but repetitive, and the GAN approach optimizes both.
On an audience question about better benchmarks: better metrics are
one way to make progress, if you train
a coding agent to care about downstream
maintainability or security, not just whether it compiles or the user accepts
it, you align incentives better. But you're always subject to Goodhart's
law: you specify the incentive, miss something, and
the model exploits the gap. We ran a human
study with expert musicians, and the GAN model
was preferred on adaptation quality, speed, control,
and agency. To connect back to LLM writing:
you might avoid some reward hacking by requiring the
LLM's output to be indistinguishable from human writing
per a discriminator, so instead of pulling
essays into an unhuman-like space, the model stays human-like more effectively. There's a
project website, code, and audio samples. That's what
I wanted to cover, happy to take questions.
